claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity project produces high-resolution full brain images of hundreds of brains.
source: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity project produces high-resolution full brain images of hundreds of brains.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the AMBCA project's output, supported by citation to the project.

claim: A DNN-based segmentation pipeline was developed that uses autofluorescence intensities of images to segment cell nuclei even within the densest regions, such as the dentate gyrus.
source: We developed a DNN-based segmentation pipeline that uses the autofluorescence intensities of images to segment cell nuclei even within the densest regions, such as the dentate gyrus.
evidence: The development of the pipeline is described in the methods and demonstrated in figures.

claim: The pipeline was applied to 507 brains of males and females from C57BL/6J and FVB.CD1 strains.
source: We applied our pipeline to 507 brains of males and females from C57BL/6J and FVB.CD1 strains.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size and composition, confirmed in Table 1.

claim: Increased overall brain volume does not result in uniform expansion across all regions.
source: Globally, we found that increased overall brain volume does not result in uniform expansion across all regions.
evidence: This finding is supported by data analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Region-specific density changes are often negatively correlated with the volume of the region.
source: Moreover, region-specific density changes are often negatively correlated with the volume of the region; therefore, cell count does not scale linearly with volume.
evidence: This is demonstrated through correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cell count does not scale linearly with volume.
source: Moreover, region-specific density changes are often negatively correlated with the volume of the region; therefore, cell count does not scale linearly with volume.
evidence: This conclusion follows from the negative correlation between density and volume.

claim: Many regions, including layer 2/3 across several cortical areas, showed distinct lateral bias.
source: Many regions, including layer 2/3 across several cortical areas, showed distinct lateral bias.
evidence: This is supported by laterality analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: Males tended to have more cells in extended amygdala and hypothalamic regions (MEA, BST, BLA, BMA, and LPO, AHN).
source: For example, males tended to have more cells in extended amygdala and hypothalamic regions (MEA, BST, BLA, BMA, and LPO, AHN) while females had more cells in the orbital cortex (ORB).
evidence: This sex difference is demonstrated in Figure 4 with statistical testing.

claim: Females had more cells in the orbital cortex (ORB).
source: For example, males tended to have more cells in extended amygdala and hypothalamic regions (MEA, BST, BLA, BMA, and LPO, AHN) while females had more cells in the orbital cortex (ORB).
evidence: This sex difference is demonstrated in Figure 4 with statistical testing.

claim: Inter-individual variability was always greater than the effect size of a single qualifier.
source: Yet, inter-individual variability was always greater than the effect size of a single qualifier.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the population analysis throughout the results.

claim: The mouse brain is by far the most intensively studied among mammalian brains.
source: The mouse brain is by far the most intensively studied among mammalian brains, yet basic measures of its cytoarchitecture remain obscure.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Basic measures of mouse brain cytoarchitecture remain obscure.
source: The mouse brain is by far the most intensively studied among mammalian brains, yet basic measures of its cytoarchitecture remain obscure.
evidence: This statement motivates the study and is supported by the lack of comprehensive data in the literature.

claim: Quantifying cell numbers, and the interplay of sex, strain, and individual variability in cell density and volume is out of reach for many regions.
source: For example, quantifying cell numbers, and the interplay of sex, strain, and individual variability in cell density and volume is out of reach for many regions.
evidence: This describes a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The mammalian brain can be divided into neuroanatomical units characterized by a shared function, connectivity, developmental origin, and/or cytoarchitecture.
source: The mammalian brain can be divided into neuroanatomical units (i.e., brain regions) characterized by a shared function, connectivity, developmental origin, and/or cytoarchitecture (i.e., number and density of cells it contains).
evidence: This is a foundational statement about brain organization based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Few studies have systematically mapped cell bodies or quantified cell densities in mouse brains, compared to the early, detailed cell mapping of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Although cytoarchitecture is one of the most prominent features of a brain region, few studies have systematically mapped cell bodies or quantified cell densities in mouse brains, compared to the early, detailed cell mapping of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to the C. elegans work and describes the state of the field.

claim: Extensive literature explored scaling of cell numbers and densities among mammalian brains.
source: On the other hand, extensive literature explored scaling of cell numbers and densities among mammalian brains (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006; Herculano-Houzel and Lent, 2005; Azevedo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Previous scaling studies were performed by counting dissociated nuclei at the loss of deeper region-specific resolution.
source: This however was performed by counting dissociated nuclei at the loss of deeper region-specific resolution.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous approaches, based on knowledge of the methods used.

claim: Obtaining an accurate cell count for a brain region is technically challenging.
source: Obtaining an accurate cell count for a brain region is technically challenging.
evidence: This is a general statement about the difficulty of the task, supported by the subsequent discussion of limitations.

claim: Previous estimates relied heavily on extrapolation from manual counting of 2D sections (stereology), making cell-resolved data for subcortical regions sparse.
source: Previous estimates relied heavily on extrapolation from manual counting of 2D sections (stereology), making cell-resolved data for subcortical regions sparse (Keller et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes limitations of previous methods, supported by citation.

claim: Analyzing complete brains using 2D histological sections remains labor-intensive because it requires sectioning, mounting, and accurate alignment with a reference atlas.
source: Analyzing complete brains using 2D histological sections remains labor-intensive because it requires sectioning, mounting, and accurate alignment with a reference atlas.
evidence: This describes practical limitations of traditional methods based on established knowledge.

claim: Automated cell counting proved particularly difficult in dense regions, such as the hippocampal formation (HPF) and the cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, automated cell counting proved particularly difficult in dense regions, such as the hippocampal formation (HPF) and the cerebellum (Attili et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to relevant literature.

claim: Automated block-face imaging methods solved several issues and drastically improved throughput.
source: Automated block-face imaging methods solved several of these issues and drastically improved throughput (Ueda et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to relevant literature.

claim: Serial two-photon tomography (STPT) was a technological breakthrough that integrated tissue sectioning with top-view light microscopy.
source: For instance, serial two-photon tomography (STPT) (Ragan et al., 2012) was a technological breakthrough that integrated tissue sectioning with top-view light microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original STPT paper.

claim: STPT provided high-quality imaging in an optical plane below the sectioning surface and solved many problems of section distortion and atlas alignment.
source: STPT provided high-quality imaging in an optical plane below the sectioning surface and solved many problems of section distortion and atlas alignment, further easing downstream analysis.
evidence: This describes advantages of STPT based on the cited literature and general knowledge.

claim: STPT typically represents a subsample of the complete volume, and some interpolation is needed.
source: Yet, STPT typically represents a subsample of the complete volume, and some interpolation is needed.
evidence: This describes a limitation of STPT based on how the method works.

claim: Histological studies cannot supply the number of analyzed brains needed to uncover potential variability between individuals, experimental conditions, and populations because of their limited throughput.
source: Because of their limited throughput, histological studies cannot supply the number of analyzed brains needed to uncover potential variability between individuals, experimental conditions, and populations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of traditional methods.

claim: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can measure some features, such as the volume of given brain regions, and can even track individuals over time in a noninvasive manner.
source: Complementary approaches aimed at evaluating variability, for example, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can measure some features, such as the volume of given brain regions, and can even track individuals over time in a noninvasive manner.
evidence: This describes capabilities of MRI based on established knowledge.

claim: MRI lacks the accuracy needed for counting cells or assessing cell densities.
source: Yet, MRI lacks the accuracy needed for counting cells or assessing cell densities, and it remains difficult to simultaneously analyze regional volume and cell density with high accuracy brain-wide, especially in the large throughput required for comparing two experimental populations (such as two strains, or males vs. females).
evidence: This describes limitations of MRI based on established knowledge.

claim: It remains difficult to simultaneously analyze regional volume and cell density with high accuracy brain-wide, especially in the large throughput required for comparing two experimental populations.
source: Yet, MRI lacks the accuracy needed for counting cells or assessing cell densities, and it remains difficult to simultaneously analyze regional volume and cell density with high accuracy brain-wide, especially in the large throughput required for comparing two experimental populations (such as two strains, or males vs. females).
evidence: This describes a gap in current methods that motivates the study.

claim: The AMBCA dataset is the largest existing cohort of whole-brain STPT images.
source: To address this knowledge gap, we harnessed the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Project (AMBCA) dataset, which is largest existing cohort of whole-brain STPT images, produced by the Allen Institute for the different purpose of mapping mouse regional connectivity (Oh et al., 2014; http://help.brain-map.org/display/api/Allen%2BBrain%2BAtlas%2BAPI).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the AMBCA dataset, supported by citation.

claim: The AMBCA dataset was produced by the Allen Institute for the purpose of mapping mouse regional connectivity.
source: To address this knowledge gap, we harnessed the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Project (AMBCA) dataset, which is largest existing cohort of whole-brain STPT images, produced by the Allen Institute for the different purpose of mapping mouse regional connectivity (Oh et al., 2014; http://help.brain-map.org/display/api/Allen%2BBrain%2BAtlas%2BAPI).
evidence: This describes the original purpose of the AMBCA dataset, supported by citation.

claim: A deep neural network (DNN) was applied to discern cell nuclei using the AMBCA background autofluorescence channel.
source: We applied a deep neural network (DNN) to discern cell nuclei using the AMBCA background autofluorescence channel.
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: The DNN enabled systematic brain-wide cell density estimation across hundreds of mouse brains.
source: This enabled us to perform a systematic brain-wide cell density estimation across hundreds of mouse brains.
evidence: This describes the outcome of applying the DNN method.

claim: Based on the alignment with the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (AMBA), volume and density were measured for each brain, for each region, over a large population.
source: Based on the alignment with the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (AMBA), we were able to simultaneously measure volume and density for each brain, for each region, over a large population.
evidence: This describes the data collection approach.

claim: A comprehensive database was constructed that aggregates the results and provides them as an accessible resource to the community.
source: We constructed a comprehensive database that aggregates these results and provides them as an accessible resource to the community.
evidence: This describes a deliverable of the study.

claim: Nontrivial relationships between densities and volumes were discovered.
source: We also discovered nontrivial relationships between densities and volumes, and gained insights into strain- and sex-dependent characteristics across various brain regions.
evidence: This summarizes findings from the analysis.

claim: Insights into strain- and sex-dependent characteristics across various brain regions were gained.
source: We also discovered nontrivial relationships between densities and volumes, and gained insights into strain- and sex-dependent characteristics across various brain regions.
evidence: This summarizes findings from the analysis.

claim: The red (background) channel of STPT images features dark, round-like objects resembling cell nuclei.
source: We noticed that the red (background) channel of STPT images, taken for the purpose of atlas alignment, typically features dark, round-like objects resembling cell nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from the images.

claim: This phenomenon of dark objects in autofluorescence images was described in previous literature.
source: This phenomenon was described in previous literature (Wang et al., 2020; Costantini et al., 2021; DaCosta et al., 2005; Kretschmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Zipfel et al., 2003 characterized the use of multiphoton-excited native florescence and second harmonic generation for the purpose of staining-free tissue imaging.
source: In particular, Zipfel et al., 2003 characterized the use of multiphoton-excited native florescence and second harmonic generation for the purpose of staining-free tissue imaging.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Zipfel paper.

claim: 91–98% of detected objects were also marked by DAPI, confirming that dark objects in STPT indeed represent cell nuclei.
source: 91–98% of detected objects were also marked by DAPI, confirming that dark objects in STPT indeed represent cell nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result comparing autofluorescence detection with DAPI staining.

claim: About 2–9% of detected low-autofluorescent objects were additional 'false positive' detections that were not obvious in the DAPI image.
source: About 2–9% of detected low-autofluorescent objects were additional 'false positive' detections that were not obvious in the DAPI image.
evidence: This quantifies the false positive rate from the validation experiment.

claim: 26–45% of DAPI-detected nuclei were not observed in the autofluorescent images (false negatives), pointing to an underestimate of cell counts based on low-autofluorescence objects, compared to nuclear staining.
source: On the other hand, 26–45% of DAPI-detected nuclei were not observed in the autofluorescent images (false negatives), pointing to an underestimate of cell counts based on low-autofluorescence objects, compared to nuclear staining.
evidence: This quantifies the false negative rate and its implication for cell count estimates.

claim: The DNN model performed with an estimated 97% cell detection accuracy on a test set, with a false positive rate of <0.01.
source: The model performed with an estimated 97% cell detection accuracy on a test set, with a false positive rate of <0.01 (see 'Methods') whenever image quality was sufficient (for exclusion criteria of whole brains or certain regions within sections, see 'Methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative performance metric from model evaluation.

claim: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain contained a total of 76 ± 11 × 10^6 cells.
source: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain contained a total of 76 ± 11 × 106 cells, in 380 mm3 of gray matter, at a density of 2.05 × 105 cells/mm3.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain contained 380 mm^3 of gray matter.
source: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain contained a total of 76 ± 11 × 106 cells, in 380 mm3 of gray matter, at a density of 2.05 × 105 cells/mm3.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain had a cell density of 2.05 × 10^5 cells/mm^3.
source: The median male C57BL/6J mouse brain contained a total of 76 ± 11 × 106 cells, in 380 mm3 of gray matter, at a density of 2.05 × 105 cells/mm3.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Good correlation (ρ = 0.86 and ρ = 0.98 for log and linear scale, respectively; interclass correlation coefficient 0.98–0.99) was found with a recent 3D whole-brain single-cell resolved light-sheet microscopy study.
source: We quantified each level of the hierarchical tree structure of the AMBA and found good correlation (ρ = 0.86 and ρ = 0.98 for log and linear scale, respectively; interclass correlation coefficient 0.98–0.99) with a recent 3D whole-brain single-cell resolved light-sheet microscopy study (Murakami et al., 2018; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with an independent study, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The diameter of detected objects (nuclei) varied between 7 and 9.5 μm.
source: The diameter of detected objects (nuclei) varied between 7 and 9.5 μm (Figure 2E, left), which at a nucleus/soma volumetric ratio of 0.08 (Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Huber and Gerace, 2007) corresponds to median cell body diameters from 16.25 μm in the RSPv6a, to 22 μm in the ENTl3.
evidence: This is a measurement from the data, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At a nucleus/soma volumetric ratio of 0.08, nucleus diameters of 7-9.5 μm correspond to median cell body diameters from 16.25 μm in the RSPv6a, to 22 μm in the ENTl3.
source: The diameter of detected objects (nuclei) varied between 7 and 9.5 μm (Figure 2E, left), which at a nucleus/soma volumetric ratio of 0.08 (Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Huber and Gerace, 2007) corresponds to median cell body diameters from 16.25 μm in the RSPv6a, to 22 μm in the ENTl3.
evidence: This is a calculation based on measured nucleus size and cited nucleus/soma ratio.

claim: Regional variability of cell densities was high, ranging from 1 × 10^5 mm^-3 in layer 1 isocortex (e.g., Mos1) to 6 × 10^5 mm^-3 in the dentate gyrus granule layer (DG-sg).
source: The regional variability of cell densities was high, ranging from 1 × 105 mm–3 in layer 1 isocortex (e.g., Mos1) to 6 × 105 mm–3 in the dentate gyrus granule layer (DG-sg).
evidence: This describes the range of measured densities across regions.

claim: FVB.CD1 males had a 7.6% larger gray matter volume (GMV) than C57BL/6J males.
source: FVB.CD1, however, had a 7.6% larger gray matter volume (GMV) than C57BL/6J.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between strains shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FVB.CD1 males had an ~10% increase in the median cell count compared to C57BL/6J males.
source: Combining these two features revealed an ~10% increase in the median cell count in FVB.CD1 vs. C57BL/6J (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between strains shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Median cell density was similar for C57BL/6J and FVB.CD1 male strains, with considerably larger variance in FVB.CD1 males.
source: Median cell density was similar for the two strains, with considerably larger variance in FVB.CD1 males.
evidence: This is a comparison of distributions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is no simple relationship between volume and density, therefore, both properties should be measured simultaneously.
source: These results suggest that (1) there is no simple relationship between volume and density, therefore, both properties should be measured simultaneously; and (2) a large cohort enables detection of relatively small differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the strain comparison data.

claim: A large cohort enables detection of relatively small differences.
source: These results suggest that (1) there is no simple relationship between volume and density, therefore, both properties should be measured simultaneously; and (2) a large cohort enables detection of relatively small differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the power of large sample sizes.

claim: Correlation between in-house Hoechst dataset and AMBCA analysis was very high when comparing the volume across regions (ρ = 0.99).
source: As expected, correlation between this in-house dataset and the AMBCA analysis was very high when comparing the volume across regions (ρ = 0.99, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result comparing two methods.

claim: Cell count correlations between Hoechst and AMBCA were high (ρ = 0.99), but median cell count in Hoechst was 65% higher.
source: In addition, cell count correlations were also high (ρ = 0.99, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), but median cell count in Hoechst was 65% higher; recapitulating the trend toward false negatives observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (epifluorescence microscopy).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between methods.

claim: The pyramidal layer of CA1 was denser than that of CA3 and CA2.
source: Analyzing 195 C57BL/6J male brains, we found that the pyramidal layer of CA1 was denser than that of CA3 and CA2, whereas nucleus size was larger in CA3.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of hippocampal regions.

claim: Nucleus size was larger in CA3 than in CA1 and CA2.
source: Analyzing 195 C57BL/6J male brains, we found that the pyramidal layer of CA1 was denser than that of CA3 and CA2, whereas nucleus size was larger in CA3.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of hippocampal regions.

claim: In the dentate gyrus, the granule layer had the highest density of all regions, with >6.5 × 10^5 cells/mm^3.
source: In the dentate gyrus, the granule layer had the highest density of all regions, with >6.5 × 105 cells/mm3, and nuclei were largest in the polymorph layer (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, upper panels).
evidence: This is a finding about the dentate gyrus from the analysis.

claim: Nuclei were largest in the polymorph layer of the dentate gyrus.
source: In the dentate gyrus, the granule layer had the highest density of all regions, with >6.5 × 105 cells/mm3, and nuclei were largest in the polymorph layer (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, upper panels).
evidence: This is a finding about the dentate gyrus from the analysis.

claim: Layer 1 of the isocortex was consistently underpopulated, having a density of about 10^5 cells/mm^3.
source: Layer 1 was consistently underpopulated, having a density of about 105 cells/mm3.
evidence: This is a finding about cortical layer 1 from the analysis.

claim: The overall rank order of cortical layer density from densest to sparsest was layer 4 > layer 6a > layer 5 > layer 2/3 > layer 1.
source: The overall rank order from densest to sparsest was maintained, with layer 4 > layer 6a > layer 5 > layer 2/3 > layer 1, suggesting a similarity in cytoarchitecture between cortical regions.
evidence: This is a finding about cortical layer organization from the analysis.

claim: The rank order of cortical layer densities suggests a similarity in cytoarchitecture between cortical regions.
source: The overall rank order from densest to sparsest was maintained, with layer 4 > layer 6a > layer 5 > layer 2/3 > layer 1, suggesting a similarity in cytoarchitecture between cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the consistent rank order across regions.

claim: Layer 4 of the primary visual and somatosensory cortices had higher density than did the auditory and visceral cortices.
source: Layer 4 of the primary visual and somatosensory cortices had higher density than did the auditory and visceral cortices.
evidence: This is a finding about regional differences in layer 4 density.

claim: In C57BL/6J (n = 369), 229 regions were found with lateral cell density bias of over 5%, and up to 30%.
source: In C57BL/6J (n = 369), we found 229 regions with lateral cell density bias of over 5%, and up to 30%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about laterality from the analysis.

claim: Both left and right hemispheres showed similar numbers of biased regions in density (left, 100; right, 129).
source: Both sides showed similar numbers of biased regions in density (left, 100; right, 129, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the distribution of laterality.

claim: Neighboring regions in prefrontal cortex ACAv2/3, ACAd2/3, ORBl2/3, and PL/23 were up to 30% denser in the right hemisphere.
source: Neighboring regions in prefrontal cortex ACAv2/3, ACAd2/3, ORBl2/3, and PL/23 were up to 30% denser in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a specific finding about prefrontal cortex laterality.

claim: The parasubiculum (PAR) showed a consistent per-brain higher cell density in the right hemisphere.
source: In addition, a more posterior part of the HPF, the parasubiculum (PAR) also showed a consistent per-brain higher cell density in the right hemisphere (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a specific finding about PAR laterality.

claim: Cortical areas GU2/3, RSPv6a, VISC2/3, and AUDv2/3 showed more than 20% higher density in the left hemisphere.
source: In contrast, cortical areas GU2/3, RSPv6a, VISC2/3, and AUDv2/3 showed more than 20% higher density in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a specific finding about left hemisphere density bias.

claim: Consistent density bias was found in left hemisphere cortical regions, specifically in layers 2/3.
source: Strikingly, we found consistent density bias in left hemisphere cortical regions, specifically in layers 2/3 (Figure 3A, upper inset).
evidence: This is a finding about layer-specific laterality.

claim: The density bias was both most consistent and pronounced in a group of neighboring ventrolateral areas: visceral, gustatory, temporal association, and auditory.
source: This bias was both most consistent and pronounced in a group of neighboring ventrolateral areas: visceral, gustatory, temporal association, and auditory (Figure 3C), where the latter may be consistent with the Levy et al. findings.
evidence: This is a finding about regional patterns of laterality.

claim: The laterality in auditory cortex may be consistent with the Levy et al. findings.
source: This bias was both most consistent and pronounced in a group of neighboring ventrolateral areas: visceral, gustatory, temporal association, and auditory (Figure 3C), where the latter may be consistent with the Levy et al. findings.
evidence: This is a speculation connecting the current findings to previous literature.

claim: Laterally biased regions were consistent across strains (e.g., C57BL/6J vs. FVB.CD1).
source: Laterally biased regions were consistent across strains (e.g., C57BL/6J vs. FVB.CD1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding about the consistency of laterality across strains.

claim: Volume laterality was less pronounced than density laterality, with some regions slightly larger in the right hemisphere.
source: We note that volume laterality was less pronounced with some regions slightly larger in the right hemisphere (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding comparing laterality in volume vs. density.

claim: Most regions did not show laterality in both density and volume.
source: Most regions did not show laterality in both density and volume (e.g., PAR and VISC2/3 in Figure 3B and D display density laterality, while no bias in volume is observed).
evidence: This is a finding about the independence of density and volume laterality.

claim: Differences between males and females in regional neuroanatomy have been extensively described, including dimorphic volume and cell count in the medial amygdala (MEA) and in the bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BST).
source: Differences between males and females in regional neuroanatomy have been extensively described, including dimorphic volume and cell count in the medial amygdala (MEA) (Morris et al., 2008; Morris et al., 2005) and in the bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BST) (Garcia-Falgueras et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about existing literature on sexual dimorphism, supported by citations.

claim: At the global level (whole-brain gray matter), C57BL/6J males and females had similar volume (380 ± 17 mm^3 and 380 ± 14 mm^3, for females and males, respectively).
source: Although at the global level (whole-brain gray matter), males and females had similar volume (380 ± 17 mm3 and 380 ± 14 mm3, for females and males, respectively), in density (1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 and 1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 for females and males, respectively) and total numbers of cells (75 ± 10 × 106 and 77 ± 9 × 106 for females and males, respectively) (Figure 4A), certain regions displayed sexual dimorphism in one or more property.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between sexes at the whole-brain level.

claim: At the global level, C57BL/6J males and females had similar density (1.97 ± 0.28 × 10^5 cells/mm^3 for both).
source: Although at the global level (whole-brain gray matter), males and females had similar volume (380 ± 17 mm3 and 380 ± 14 mm3, for females and males, respectively), in density (1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 and 1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 for females and males, respectively) and total numbers of cells (75 ± 10 × 106 and 77 ± 9 × 106 for females and males, respectively) (Figure 4A), certain regions displayed sexual dimorphism in one or more property.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between sexes at the whole-brain level.

claim: At the global level, C57BL/6J males and females had similar total numbers of cells (75 ± 10 × 10^6 and 77 ± 9 × 10^6 for females and males, respectively).
source: Although at the global level (whole-brain gray matter), males and females had similar volume (380 ± 17 mm3 and 380 ± 14 mm3, for females and males, respectively), in density (1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 and 1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 for females and males, respectively) and total numbers of cells (75 ± 10 × 106 and 77 ± 9 × 106 for females and males, respectively) (Figure 4A), certain regions displayed sexual dimorphism in one or more property.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between sexes at the whole-brain level.

claim: Certain regions displayed sexual dimorphism in one or more property (volume, density, or count).
source: Although at the global level (whole-brain gray matter), males and females had similar volume (380 ± 17 mm3 and 380 ± 14 mm3, for females and males, respectively), in density (1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 and 1.97 ± 0.28 × 105 cells/mm3 for females and males, respectively) and total numbers of cells (75 ± 10 × 106 and 77 ± 9 × 106 for females and males, respectively) (Figure 4A), certain regions displayed sexual dimorphism in one or more property.
evidence: This is a summary statement about regional sexual dimorphism.

claim: MEA and BST, but also the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCO), taenia tecta ventral (TTv), and the medial preoptic nucleus (MPN) were >5% larger in males.
source: Most regions were consistent with the overall trend of equal volume, yet MEA and BST, but also the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCO), taenia tecta ventral (TTv), and the medial preoptic nucleus (MPN) were >5% larger in males.
evidence: This is a finding about regions with larger volume in males.

claim: Ventrolateral orbital area layer 2/3 (ORBvl2/3) displayed larger volume in females.
source: A handful of regions, for example, ventrolateral orbital area layer 2/3 (ORBvl2/3), displayed the opposite effect and had larger volume in females.
evidence: This is a finding about a region with larger volume in females.

claim: ORBvl2/3 was the only region to also display significantly higher density and cell count in females.
source: ORBvl2/3 was the only region to also display significantly higher density and cell count in females.
evidence: This is a finding about ORBvl2/3 being unique in showing multiple dimorphic properties favoring females.

claim: Many regions were 5–20% denser in males, including other parts of the amygdala (BMA, BLA, and the CEA), hypothalamic regions LPO and AHN, and cortical regions such as the primary auditory layer 2/3 (AUDv2/3).
source: In contrast, many regions were 5–20% denser in males, which also resulted in higher cell counts. These regions include other parts of the amygdala (BMA, BLA, and the CEA), hypothalamic regions LPO and AHN, and cortical regions such as the primary auditory layer 2/3 (AUDv2/3).
evidence: This is a finding about regions with higher density in males.

claim: In an independent AMBCA cohort of additional 663 males and 166 females, findings regarding region-specific sexual dimorphism were robustly replicated: volumes of MEA, BST, and ORBvl2/3 displayed sex differences of consistent effect size and variance.
source: In an independent AMBCA cohort of additional 663 males and 166 females, we could robustly replicate our findings regarding region-specific sexual dimorphism: volumes of MEA, BST, and ORBvl2/3 displayed sex differences of consistent effect size and variance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is a validation of findings in an independent cohort.

claim: Using volume data, MEA and BST alone performed sex classification to >78% accuracy.
source: Using volume data, MEA and BST alone performed classification to >78% accuracy.
evidence: This is a result from the SVM classification analysis.

claim: Adding the postpiriform transitional area (TR) and the rostral lateral septal nucleus (LSr) to MEA and BST, the volume-based classifier's performance saturated to about 90%.
source: Adding the postpiriform transitional area (TR) and the rostral lateral septal nucleus (LSr), the classifier's performance saturated to about 90% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a result from the SVM classification analysis.

claim: The density-based classifier showed only incremental improvements when adding almost any of the top 10 regions.
source: In contrast, the density-based classifier showed only incremental improvements when adding almost any of the top 10 regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a result from the SVM classification analysis comparing density vs. volume.

claim: Although many brain regions show significant differences between males and females both in volume and density, the considerable overlap between the male and female population distributions in each of these regions hampers classification.
source: Together, these results suggest that although many brain regions show significant differences between males and females both in volume and density (Figure 4), the considerable overlap between the male and female population distributions in each of these regions hampers classification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results.

claim: Apart from MEA and BST, the volume-based classifier revealed TR, LSr, MPN, and ORBl2/3 as predictors for sex.
source: Apart from MEA and BST, the classifier revealed TR, LSr, MPN, and ORBl2/3 as predictors for sex based on volume, while density-based classification was based on amygdala-related regions (COApl, BMAp) and frontal cortical regions (ILA and ORB).
evidence: This is a result from the SVM classification analysis.

claim: Density-based sex classification was based on amygdala-related regions (COApl, BMAp) and frontal cortical regions (ILA and ORB).
source: Apart from MEA and BST, the classifier revealed TR, LSr, MPN, and ORBl2/3 as predictors for sex based on volume, while density-based classification was based on amygdala-related regions (COApl, BMAp) and frontal cortical regions (ILA and ORB).
evidence: This is a result from the SVM classification analysis.

claim: In both C57BL/6J and FVB.CD1 strains, males and females showed distinct distributions for body weight, and males were larger than females.
source: As expected, in both strains, males and females showed distinct distributions for body weight, and males were larger than females (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding about body weight differences between sexes.

claim: Within each strain, body weight did not correlate with gray volume.
source: Within each strain, body weight did not correlate with gray volume.
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of correlation between body weight and brain volume.

claim: FVB.CD1 brains were overall larger, but the volume expansion with respect to C57BL/6J was not uniform across regions.
source: FVB.CD1 brains were overall larger, but the volume expansion with respect to C57BL/6J was not uniform across regions.
evidence: This is a finding about strain differences in regional volume.

claim: Region volumes ranged up to 30% differences between strains, with the extreme example of the cerebellum (CENT2), whose size increased by 45% in both FVB.CD1 males and females.
source: Region volumes ranged up to 30% differences, with the extreme example of the cerebellum (CENT2), whose size increased by 45% in both FVB.CD1 males and females (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding about the magnitude of strain differences in regional volume.

claim: Per-region volume differences between strains were, in general, larger in males.
source: Moreover, per-region volume differences between strains were, in general, larger in males (i.e., most data points in Figure 5B quadrant III are above the diagonal).
evidence: This is a finding about sex-specific strain differences.

claim: Only two regions showed larger volumes in C57BL/6J: the main olfactory bulb (MOB) and the lateral amygdalar nucleus (LA).
source: Only two regions showed larger volumes in C57BL/6J: the main olfactory bulb (MOB) and the lateral amygdalar nucleus (LA) (Figure 5B, quadrant I).
evidence: This is a finding about regions that are larger in C57BL/6J.

claim: Most regions were denser in FVB.CD1 compared to C57BL/6J.
source: A similar comparison for cell density per region suggests nonuniform density differences, with most regions being denser in FVB.CD1 (Figure 5B, quadrant III).
evidence: This is a finding about strain differences in density.

claim: Olfaction-related regions (AOB and MOB) showed higher density in C57BL/6J.
source: Notably, olfaction-related regions (AOB and MOB) showed higher density in C57BL/6J.
evidence: This is a finding about specific regions with higher density in C57BL/6J.

claim: Sexual dimorphism in MEA and BST, which were larger in males, was more pronounced in FVB.CD1 than in C57BL/6J.
source: Differences in volume confirmed sexual dimorphism in MEA and BST, which were larger in males for both strains. These differences were more pronounced in FVB.CD1 than in C57BL/6J (Figure 5D, quadrant I).
evidence: This is a finding about strain-specific differences in sexual dimorphism.

claim: Many brain regions showed 'strain-discordant' dimorphism, with females having a larger volume in C57BL/6J and males in FVB.CD1.
source: Many brain regions showed 'strain-discordant' dimorphism, with females having a larger volume in C57BL/6J and males in FVB.CD1 (Figure 5D, quadrant II).
evidence: This is a finding about complex interactions between strain and sex.

claim: In both strains, males had higher density in most regions (except for, e.g., ORBvl2/3).
source: Comparing sexual dimorphism in density (Figure 5E), we found a simpler and more consistent picture: in both strains, males had higher density in most regions (except for, e.g., ORBvl2/3).
evidence: This is a finding about sex differences in density across strains.

claim: Sex differences in density were found to be larger in FVB.CD1 than in C57BL/6J.
source: Note that in density as well, sex differences were found to be larger in FVB.CD1 (most data points in Figure 5E, quadrant I, are above the diagonal).
evidence: This is a finding about strain-specific differences in sexual dimorphism of density.

claim: In 79% of regions (356/451), cell density was negatively correlated with volume.
source: Based on per-region measurements of both V and D, we calculated regionally resolved Pearson correlations between volume and density in C57BL/6J (Figure 6B). In 79% of regions (356/451), cell density was negatively correlated with volume (Figure 6C), with a median correlation of –0.14.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the relationship between volume and density.

claim: The median correlation between cell density and volume across regions was –0.14.
source: Based on per-region measurements of both V and D, we calculated regionally resolved Pearson correlations between volume and density in C57BL/6J (Figure 6B). In 79% of regions (356/451), cell density was negatively correlated with volume (Figure 6C), with a median correlation of –0.14.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the relationship between volume and density.

claim: Across regions cell count does not scale uniformly with volume.
source: This suggests that across regions cell count does not scale uniformly with volume.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the variable correlations between density and volume.

claim: The density-based tSNE embedding map reveals clear 2D 'clusters,' largely consistent with neuroanatomical classification.
source: The density-based tSNE embedding map in Figure 6F reveals clear 2D 'clusters,' largely consistent with neuroanatomical classification.
evidence: This is a finding from the tSNE analysis of density data.

claim: Cortical regions appear in the upper part of the density-based tSNE map, and cerebellum, midbrain, and hindbrain in the lower part.
source: Cortical regions appear in the upper part of the map (colored green), and cerebellum (yellow), midbrain, and hindbrain in the lower part.
evidence: This describes the organization of the tSNE map shown in Figure 6F.

claim: tSNE embedding based on volume was more 'dispersed' and displayed disorder with respect to neuroanatomical classification compared to density-based embedding.
source: Compared to Figure 6F, tSNE embedding based on volume was more 'dispersed' and displayed disorder with respect to neuroanatomical classification (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a comparison between density-based and volume-based tSNE embeddings.

claim: Similarity in volume across regions is less 'preserved' brain-wide than similarity in cell density.
source: Thus, similarity in volume across regions is less 'preserved' brain-wide than similarity in cell density.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tSNE and correlation analyses.

claim: The study has several limitations including that the model is sensitive to the contrast between dark nuclei and autofluorescent surroundings, which can be limited by image quality and tissue composition.
source: The study has several limitations. First, the model is sensitive to the contrast between dark nuclei and autofluorescent surroundings, which can be limited by image quality and tissue composition.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method.

claim: The staining-free approach depends on the presence of intrinsic molecular indicators such as NADH, retinol, or collagen, which may vary between cell or tissue components, even within the brain.
source: In particular, the staining-free approach depends on the presence of intrinsic molecular indicators such as NADH, retinol, or collagen (Zipfel et al., 2003), which may vary between cell or tissue components, even within the brain.
evidence: This is a stated limitation based on the biology of autofluorescence, supported by citation.

claim: In the hindbrain (pons, medulla), contrast was exceedingly weak, and quantifications in this region are expected to be 66% of the value estimated by nuclear staining.
source: In the hindbrain (pons, medulla), contrast was exceedingly weak, and we expect our quantifications in this region to be 66% of the value estimated by nuclear staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a stated limitation with quantified underestimation based on comparison data.

claim: AMBA annotations were not always resolved to the most refined level of the atlas hierarchy.
source: Second, AMBA annotations were not always resolved to the most refined level of the atlas hierarchy.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the atlas annotations.

claim: Density values for the cerebellum appear to be uncharacteristic because the cell-dense granule layer and sparse molecular layer were not distinguished at the deepest level of annotation.
source: For example, density values for the cerebellum appear to be uncharacteristic because the cell-dense granule layer and sparse molecular layer were not distinguished at the deepest level of annotation (e.g., CENT3 included the granular and molecular layers).
evidence: This is a stated limitation affecting cerebellar measurements.

claim: Regions at the anterior–posterior edges (olfactory bulb and cerebellum) appear partially truncated, and their parameters are likely underestimated.
source: Third, regions at the anterior–posterior edges, that is, olfactory bulb (MOB) and cerebellum (CB), appear partially truncated, and we likely report an underestimate of their parameters.
evidence: This is a stated limitation affecting specific regions.

claim: MOB and CB volumes displayed slightly higher variance than more interior regions with similar volume.
source: MOB and CB volumes also displayed slightly higher variance than more interior regions with similar volume.
evidence: This is an observation about the quality of measurements in edge regions.

claim: In regions rich with non-neuronal cells the error of autofluorescent-based counting was larger compared to nuclear staining.
source: Indeed, in regions rich with non-neuronal cells the error of autofluorescent-based counting was larger compared to nuclear staining.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison between autofluorescence and nuclear staining.

claim: One may speculate that autofluorescent-based detection is biased for neurons.
source: Hence, one may speculate that autofluorescent-based detection is biased for neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation about the source of detection bias.

claim: The median cell counts between sexes and strains differed no more than 13% overall, or ~40% for the most deviant individual structures (MOB and CENT2), while the standard deviation across individuals was ~10 million cells (for C57BL/6J male alone).
source: The median cell counts between sexes and strains differed no more than 13% overall, or ~40% for the most deviant individual structures (MOB and CENT2), while the standard deviation across individuals was ~10 million cells (for C57BL/6J male alone).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of variability in the dataset.

claim: The notion of 'ground truth' values of brain cell number can be reached, yet are best reflected by a population distribution.
source: We claim that the notion of 'ground truth' values of brain cell number can be reached, yet are best reflected by a population distribution.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about how to interpret cell count measurements.

claim: The cohort provides the first brain-wide survey of cell architecture laterality.
source: For example, our cohort provides the first brain-wide survey of cell architecture laterality, with numerous regions showing density bias to the right or left hemisphere; and some volume bias in favor of the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the laterality findings.

claim: Sexual dimorphism of brain regions was significant, as exemplified by the success of the SVM-classifier, yet the ability to separate males from females was limited due to population's interindividual differences.
source: Sexual dimorphism of brain regions was significant, as exemplified by the success of our SVM-classifier, yet the ability to separate males from females was limited due to population's interindividual differences.
evidence: This is a summary of the sexual dimorphism findings and their interpretation.

claim: Medial amygdala and bed nuclei of the stria terminalis were both larger and denser in males, but to a lesser extent than reported in smaller studies and to a similar extent to what was reported in MRI-based studies.
source: For instance, medial amygdala and bed nuclei of the stria terminalis were both larger and denser in males, but to a lesser extent than reported in smaller studies (Cooke et al., 2007) and to a similar extent to what was reported in MRI-based studies (Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: In females, several prefrontal cortex structures were larger (e.g., ORBvl2/3), which resulted in higher cell counts.
source: By contrast, in females, several prefrontal cortex structures were larger (e.g., ORBvl2/3), which resulted in higher cell counts.
evidence: This is a finding about female-biased regions.

claim: No evidence of larger prefrontal cortex in females was found in the literature on mice, but an MRI population study of 2838 human individuals found higher GMV in prefrontal areas in women.
source: We found no evidence of this phenomenon in the literature on mice, but an MRI population study of 2838 human individuals found higher GMV in prefrontal areas in women (Lotze et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with human literature, supported by citation.

claim: Between the strains, considerable differences were found in the olfactory system, which was larger and denser in C57BL/6J, and in the cerebellum, which was larger in FVB.CD-1.
source: Between the strains, we found considerable differences in the olfactory system, which was larger and denser in C57BL/6J, and in the cerebellum, which was larger in FVB.CD-1.
evidence: This is a summary of strain differences.

claim: The AMBCA project has systematically imaged 2992 full brains, using serial two-photon tomography.
source: The AMBCA project was first published in 2014 (Oh et al., 2014). The project has systematically imaged 2992 full brains, using serial two-photon tomography, for the purpose of tracing neuronal projections and mapping regional (mesoscale) connectivity with GFP-labeled viral tracers.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the AMBCA dataset, supported by citation.

claim: Each brain in the AMBCA dataset is covered by 130–140 (median 137) serial coronal sections, with a gap of 100 μm.
source: Each brain in the dataset is covered by 130–140 (median 137) serial coronal sections, with a gap of 100 μm, as reported in the AMBCA study (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a technical detail about the AMBCA dataset, supported by citation.

claim: The trained DNN was applied to 507 brains.
source: The trained DNN was applied to 507 brains, as described in detail below.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset size analyzed.

claim: 507 brains were processed, of which 132 were fully discarded.
source: In sum, we processed 507 brains, of which 132 were fully discarded.
evidence: This is a statement about quality control and data exclusion.

claim: Of 690 regions in AMBA, 346 were discarded completely and another 107 were partially discarded.
source: Of 690 regions in AMBA, 346 were discarded completely and another 107 were partially discarded.
evidence: This is a statement about quality control and data exclusion at the region level.

claim: The Detectron2 deep neural network library was used, which relies on a Mask R-CNN image segmentation model with the ResNet-101 as its backbone.
source: To detect cells in an image and mark their contour, we used the Detectron2 deep neural network library (Wu et al., 2019), which relies on a Mask R-CNN image segmentation model (He et al., 2018) with the ResNet-101 (He et al., 2015) as its backbone.
evidence: This is a technical description of the DNN architecture, supported by citations.
